Chapter 5: Feynman Diagrams

5 Feynman Diagrams

5.0.1 Feynman Propagators

  • We can define the feynman propagator 𝐺𝐹(𝑥,𝑦) to be implicitly defined by

    (□𝑥+𝑚2)𝐺𝐹(𝑥,𝑦)=−𝑖𝛿4(𝑥−𝑦)

  • This provides us, in posistion space, with

    𝐺𝐹(𝑥,𝑦)=∫d4𝑝(2𝜋)4𝑖𝑝2−𝑚2+𝑖𝜀𝑒𝑖𝑝⋅(𝑥−𝑦)≡∫d4𝑝(2𝜋)4𝐺𝐹(𝑝)𝑒−𝑖𝑝𝑥−𝑦̇

    • The momentum space Feynman Propagator 𝐺𝐹(𝑝) is defined as

      𝐺𝐹(𝑝)≡𝑖𝑝2−𝑚2+𝑖𝜀

  • The Feynman propagator, which we will elaborate upon, is a very fundamental quantity that is useful in evaluating Feynman diagrams (to be more explicit, it could be one of the only ways to evaluate them).

    • In conclusion, Richard Feynman is the GOAT

Definition 5.0.1.1 (Feynman Propagator).

  • The Feynman propagator 𝐺𝐹(𝑥,𝑦) or 𝐷𝐹(𝑥,𝑦) or 𝐺𝐹(𝑥−𝑦) or 𝐷𝑥𝑦 depending on the situation is defined as the time ordered product of free fields.

    • That is,

      𝐺𝐹(𝑥,𝑦)≡⟨0|𝑇𝜙(𝑥1)𝜙(𝑥2)|0⟩=lim𝜀→0∫d4𝑝(2𝜋)41𝑘2−𝑚2+𝑖𝜀𝑒𝑖𝑘(𝑥−𝑦)

Definition 5.0.1.2 (Feynman Diagram).

A Feynman diagram is something that is used to represent particle interactions, or simplifications of them which are summed. generally to calculate the LSZ reduction for matrix elements. These matrix elements are ultimately used to calculate cross sections as seen in Cross Sections.

Definition 5.0.1.3 (Feynman Rules).

Feynman rules are a set of rules for a theory which is used to evaluate Feynman diagrams.
  • A standard set of Feynman rules that can generally apply everywhere are the following

General Position Space Feynman Rules

  • At each vertex, a factor of the interaction coupling is given
  • All lines are integrated over 𝑑3𝑥 after applying the Feynman propagator
  • The LSZ reduction formula is applied to convert this to an S-matrix element
  • Additional factors may be added if they are incoming/outgoing electrons/photons due to polarization and spin

General Momentum Space Feynman Rules (Arguably much more useful:

  • Each vertex of a Feynman Diagram gets a factor of whatever the interaction coupling is.
  • Vertices can only occur at points that satisfy interactions in the Lagrangian1

  • For each edge whose momentum is known (that does not connect to an external vertex), a factor of the propagator for the theory Π is gained - For each edge whose momentum 𝑘 is unknown (i.e., a loop), a factor of Π is gained and must be integrated over

    d4𝑘(2𝜋)4.
  • The final product gives 𝑖ℳ︀ for the diagram
  • Additional factors may be added if they are incoming/outgoing electrons/photons due to polarization and spin

5.0.2 Wick’s Theorem and Feynman Diagram Derivation

  • Before diagrams, it is useful to do some calculations

    • There are two different ways to derive Feynman rules for a theory, but the most common two are through the use of lagrangians and through the use of 2nd quantization
5.0.2.1 Lagrangian Method

  • Consider Free Fields with

    [𝜙(𝒙,𝑡),𝜙(𝒙′,𝑡))]=0[𝜙(𝒙,𝑡),𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝒙′,𝑡)]=𝑖ℏ𝛿3(𝒙−𝒙′)(□+𝑚2)𝜙=0

  • We only know how to evaluate the free theory correlation functions at this point

    ⟨0|𝑇𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|0⟩

Theorem 5.0.2.1.1 (Schwinger-Dyson Equations).

  • An equation that will appear later via the use of Feynman path integrals

  • The Schwinger Dyson Equations state that

    (□+𝑚2)⟨𝜙𝑥𝜙1𝜙2…𝜙𝑛⟩=⟨ℒ︀int′[𝜙𝑥]𝜙1…𝜙𝑛⟩−𝑖ℏ∑𝑗𝛿4(𝑥−𝑥𝑗)⟨𝜙1…𝜙𝑗−1𝜙𝑗+1…𝜙𝑛⟩

    • This holds if

      ℒ︀=−12(□+𝑚2)𝜙+ℒ︀int[𝜙]

  • They differentiate classical mechanics and quantum mechanics via the ℏ term.

Proof Schwinger-Dyson Equation.

  • This should barely constitute a proof but nevertheless I have to call it something.

  • Consider

    𝜕𝑡⟨Ω|𝑇𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩

    • This is equal to

      𝜕𝑡[⟨Ω|𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩Θ(𝑡−𝑡′)+⟨Ω|𝜙(𝑥′)𝜙(𝑥)|Ω⟩Θ(𝑡′−𝑡)]=⟨Ω|𝑇𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩+⟨Ω|𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩𝜕𝑡Θ(𝑡−𝑡′)+⟨Ω|𝜙(𝑥′)𝜙(𝑥)|Ω⟩𝜕𝑡Θ(𝑡′−𝑡)

    • Using the fact that 𝜕𝑇Θ(𝑡)=𝛿(𝑡), we obtain that the above expression is equal to

      ⟨Ω|𝑇𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩+𝛿(𝑡−𝑡′)⟨Ω|[𝜙(𝑥),𝜙(𝑥′)]|Ω⟩

  • Taking the second derivative, we obtain

    𝜕𝑡2⟨Ω|𝑇𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩=⟨Ω|𝑇𝜕𝑡2𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩+𝛿(𝑡−𝑡′)⟨Ω|[𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝑥),𝜙(𝑥′)]|Ω⟩

    • Since the delta function forces time equivalence (𝑡=𝑡′) in the second term, we have that

      [𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝑥),𝜙(𝑥′)]=−𝑖ℏ𝛿3(𝒙−𝒙′)

      and therefore additionally have that

      𝜕𝑡2⟨Ω|𝑇𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩=⟨Ω|𝑇𝜕𝑡2𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)|Ω⟩−𝑖ℏ𝛿4(𝑥−𝑥′)

Chevron Notation

  • As you may have seen earlier, we have introduced notation ⟨𝜙⟩ in order to make notation more condensed. As you may be able to guess, ⟨𝜙⟩≡⟨Ω|𝜙|Ω⟩

  • Therefore, the equation with □+𝑚2 follows and implies our Feynman propagator,

    (□𝑥+𝑚2)𝐺𝐹(𝑥,𝑦)=−𝑖ℏ𝛿4(𝑥−𝑦)

  • That is,

    (□+𝑚2)⟨𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)⟩=⟨(□+𝑚2)𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)⟩−𝑖ℏ𝛿4(𝑥−𝑥′)

    • Applying Euler-Lagrange equations gives

      ⟨ℒ︀int[𝜙]′𝜙(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥′)⟩−𝑖ℏ𝛿4(𝑥−𝑥′)

  • Generalization provides the final equation,

    (□𝑥+𝑚2)𝜙=⟨ℒ︀int′𝜙𝑥𝜙1…𝜙𝑛⟩−𝑖ℏ∑𝑗⟨𝜙1…𝜙𝑗𝜙𝑗+1…𝜙𝑛⟩

⁠□

  • Now we can simply evaluate the two point functions

  • For instance,

    ⟨𝜙1𝜙2⟩=∫d4𝛿𝑥1⟨𝜙𝑥𝜙2⟩

    (this is simply using the identity that ∫d4𝑥𝛿(𝑥)𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(0).

    • The above expression is then equivalent to

      𝑖∫d4𝑥(□𝑥𝐷𝑥1)⟨𝜙𝑥𝜙2⟩=𝑖∫d4𝑥𝐷𝑥1□𝑥⟨𝜙𝑥𝜙2⟩

  • Some condensed notation was used where 𝐷𝑎𝑏=𝐺𝐹(𝑥𝑎,𝑥𝑏) and 𝛿𝑥𝑏=𝛿(𝑥−𝑥𝑏)

  • In a free theory □𝑥⟨𝜙𝑥𝜙𝑌⟩=−𝑖𝛿𝑥𝑦, and so

    ⟨𝜙1𝜙2⟩=∫d4𝑥𝐷𝑥1𝛿𝑥2=𝐷12

    which is not very interesting (it is literally a particle going from point 𝑥 to point 𝑦 without anything happening)

5.0.2.2 Wick’s Theorem/Contractions/QM Derivation
  • Let us move to an interacting theory (ℒ︀int≠0)
5.0.2.2.1 Consider the Heisenberg picture

  • We have the Heisenberg equations of motion 𝑖𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝑥)=[𝜙,𝐻]

    • These necessarily imply that 𝜙(𝒙,𝑡) evolves via an operator 𝑆. i.e.

      𝜙(𝒙,𝑡)=𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)†𝜙(𝒙)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)
      , noting that 𝑆 is the S-matrix.
    • 𝑆 satisfies 𝑖𝜕𝑡𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)=𝐻(𝑡)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0) (the schrodinger equation)

  • In the Heisenberg picture, we do not need the explicit hamiltonian, just the time dependent part

    • This is because the states are time independent and the Hamiltonian is not
  • 𝐻(𝑡)=𝐻0+𝑉(𝑡)
5.0.2.2.2 Interaction Picture

  • In the interaction picture, fields only evolve via 𝐻0

  • Free fields:

    𝜙0(𝒙,𝑡)=𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝜙(𝒙)𝑒−𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)

    • This is equivalent to the plane wave solution for scalar fields. That is,

      𝜙0(𝒙,𝑡)=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)312𝜔𝑝(𝑎𝑝𝑒−𝑖𝑝𝑥+𝑎𝑝†𝑒𝑖𝑝𝑥)

  • In order to get the real field for this, we have that

    𝜙(𝒙,𝑡)=𝑆†(𝑡,𝑡0)𝑒−𝑖𝐻(𝑡−𝑡0)𝜙0(𝒙,𝑡)𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)≡𝑈†(𝑡,𝑡0)𝜙0(𝐱,𝑡)𝑈(𝑡,𝑡0)

  • This 𝑈(𝑡,𝑡0)≡𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0) is unitary time evolution operator that we can utilize

    • It relates the Heisenberg picture to free fields at some time 𝑡

  • Notice that it satisfies (a form of) the Schrodinger equation. Namely,

    𝑖𝜕𝑡𝑈(𝑡,𝑡0)=−𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝐻0𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)+𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝐻(𝑡)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)=𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)[−𝐻0+𝐻(𝑡)]𝑒−𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)=𝐻𝐼(𝑡)𝑈(𝑡,𝑡0)

    with 𝐻𝐼(𝑡)≡𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)𝑉(𝑡)𝑒−𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)

    • This 𝐻𝐼(𝑡) is the Heisenberg interaction/potential in the interacting picture

  • The solution to this is

    𝑈(𝑡,𝑡0)=𝑇exp(−𝑖∫𝑡0𝑡𝐻𝐼(𝑡′)d𝑡′)

    which is known as the Dyson Equation

5.0.2.3 More Feynman rules derivation

  • Consider the operator

    𝑈12≡𝑈(𝑡1,𝑡2)=𝑇exp(−𝑖∫𝑡1𝑡2d𝑡′𝐻𝐼(𝑡))
    • In this notation, the later time is on the left

  • We have the following identities:

    • 𝑈21𝑈12=1
    • 𝑈−121=𝑈21†=𝑈12
    • For 𝑡1<𝑡2<𝑡3, 𝑈32𝑈21=𝑈31
    • 𝑈32𝑈12=𝑈32

  • Since 𝜙(𝑥1)=𝜙(𝒙1,𝑡)=𝑈10†𝜙0(𝒙1,𝑡)𝑈10=𝑈01𝜙0(𝒙1,𝑡)𝑈10

5.0.3 Vacuum Matrix Elements

  • We want to evolve the ground state |Ω⟩ to a time 𝑡0 such that the interacting picture and the free picture are equivalent

  • In the interacting picture, states |Ω⟩ evolve via 𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0) and are annihilated by 𝑎𝑝(𝑡) at 𝑡=−∞

  • In the heisenberg picture, 𝑎𝑝(𝑡) evolves as 𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)†𝑎𝑝(𝑡0)𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0) and annihilates |Ω⟩ at 𝑡=−∞

  • In the free theory, |0⟩ is annihilated by 𝑎𝑝

    • 𝑎𝑝 evolves only via phase rotation
    • 𝑎𝑝(𝑡0)𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)|0⟩=0 at 𝑡=−∞ (annihilation)

  • We must have that 𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)|0⟩ and 𝑆(𝑡,𝑡0)|Ω⟩ must be proportional

    • Then,

      |Ω⟩=𝒩︀𝑖lim𝑡→−∞𝑆†(𝑡,𝑡0)𝑒𝑖𝐻0(𝑡−𝑡0)|0⟩=𝒩︀𝑖𝑈0,−∞|0⟩
      -𝒩︀𝑖 is just a number

    • Similarly, for the final time,

      ⟨Ω|=𝒩︀𝐹⟨0|𝑈∞,0
      for some 𝒩︀𝑓

  • Then, for our time ordered product, assuming that 𝑡1>𝑡2>…𝑡𝑛 (WLOG), we have that

    ⟨Ω|𝑇𝜙(𝑥1)…𝜙(𝑥𝑛)|Ω⟩=⟨Ω|𝜙(𝑥1)…𝜙(𝑥𝑛)|Ω⟩=𝒩︀𝑖𝒩︀𝑓⟨0|𝑈∞0𝑈01𝜙0(𝑥1)𝑈10𝑈02𝜙0(𝑥2)𝑈20…𝑈0𝑛𝜙0(𝑥𝑛)𝑈𝑛0𝑈0−∞|0⟩=𝒩︀𝑖𝒩︀𝑓⟨0|𝑈∞1𝜙(𝑥1)𝑈12𝜙(𝑥2)𝑈23…𝑈(𝑛−1)𝑛𝜙0(𝑥𝑛)𝑈𝑛−∞|0⟩

  • Now we can simply apply the time ordering, giving

    ⟨Ω|𝑇𝜙(𝑥1)…𝜙(𝑥𝑛)|Ω⟩=𝒩︀𝑖𝒩︀𝑓⟨0|𝑇𝑈∞1𝜙0(𝑥1)𝑈12𝜙0(𝑥2)𝑈23…𝜙0(𝑥𝑛)𝑈𝑛−∞|0⟩=𝒩︀𝑖𝒩︀𝑓⟨0|𝑇𝜙0(𝑥1)…𝜙0(𝑥𝑛)𝑈∞,−∞|0⟩

  • Additionally, ⟨Ω|Ω⟩=1 which implies that, by normalization, 𝒩︀𝑖𝒩︀𝑓=⟨0|𝑈∞,−∞|0⟩−1

Note: We have been taking 𝑡→∞ this whole time, which is incorrect. Utilizing 𝑡→∞ without any damping will result in oscillations. That is, if we insert the energies

𝑒−𝑖𝐻𝑡|0⟩∑𝑛𝑒𝑖𝐸𝑛𝑡|𝑛⟩⟨𝑛|0⟩

, taking 𝑡→∞ yields 𝑒−𝑖𝑡𝐸 for an energy 𝐸 which at large times causes unpredictable phase oscillations. Thus, we must use an analytic continuation by taking 𝑡→∞−𝑖𝜀 (which would provide a dampening 𝑒−𝜀𝐸 )

  • We can finally have the time ordered product

    ⟨Ω|𝑇𝜙(𝑥1)…𝜙(𝑥𝑛)|Ω⟩=lim𝑇→∞−𝑖𝜀⟨0|𝑇𝜙0(𝑥1)…𝜙0(𝑥𝑛)exp[−𝑖∫−𝑇𝑇d𝑡𝐻𝐼(𝑡)]|0⟩⟨0|𝑇exp[−𝑖∫−𝑇𝑇d𝑡𝐻𝐼(𝑡)]|0⟩
